title: Der Bärenhäuter
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 101. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: KHM 101, closely related to the tale before it in this batch, and the source of the German word for a lazy layabout. A destitute discharged soldier strikes a seven-year bargain with the devil: he may never wash, comb his hair, cut his nails, or say a prayer, and must sleep and dress in nothing but a bearskin, but his pocket will always be full of money, and if he survives the term he keeps both his life and his fortune. Increasingly monstrous to look at, he uses his wealth to rescue an old man from debt and wins the youngest of the man’s three daughters — the only one willing to have him — before returning transformed at the end of his seven years, while the two sisters who mocked him meet a much darker end.

sentences.t: Es war einmal ein junger Kerl, der ließ sich als Soldat anwerben, hielt sich tapfer und war immer der vorderste, wenn es blaue Bohnen regnete.
sentences.l: There was once a young fellow, he let himself be enlisted as a soldier, held himself bravely and was always the foremost when it rained blue beans.
sentences.i: There was once a young fellow who let himself be enlisted as a soldier; he bore himself bravely and was always the foremost when it rained blue beans.
sentences.n: “sich anwerben lassen” = to let oneself be recruited, to take service; lassen with an infinitive gives the passive sense. “sich tapfer halten” = to bear oneself bravely. “blaue Bohnen,” blue beans, is soldiers’ slang for musket balls, so the last clause means under fire.

sentences.t: Solange der Krieg dauerte, gieng alles gut, aber als Friede geschlossen war, erhielt er seinen Abschied, und der Hauptmann sagte er könnte gehen wohin er wollte.
sentences.l: As long as the war lasted, everything went well, but when peace was concluded, he received his discharge, and the captain said he could go where he wanted.
sentences.i: As long as the war lasted all went well; but when peace was made he was given his discharge, and the captain said he might go where he pleased.
sentences.n: “Friede schließen” = to make peace, to conclude it. Abschied is a leave-taking, and of a soldier his discharge. könnte and wollte are the subjunctive of reported speech.

sentences.t: Seine Eltern waren todt, und er hatte keine Heimat mehr, da gieng er zu seinen Brüdern und bat sie möchten ihm so lange Unterhalt geben bis der Krieg wieder anfienge.
sentences.l: His parents were dead, and he had no home any more, so he went to his brothers and begged they might give him keep so long, until the war began again.
sentences.i: His parents were dead and he had no home any more, so he went to his brothers and begged them to keep him until the war should begin again.
sentences.n: Heimat is the home country, the place one belongs to, more than a house. Unterhalt is maintenance, keep — food and a roof. möchten and anfienge are reported speech; anfienge is the 1857 spelling of anfinge.

sentences.t: Die Brüder aber waren hartherzig und sagten „was sollen wir mit dir? wir können dich nicht brauchen, sieh zu wie du dich durchschlägst.“
sentences.l: The brothers, however, were hard-hearted and said “what are we to do with you? we cannot use you, see to it how you fight your way through.”
sentences.i: But the brothers were hard-hearted and said: “what are we to do with you? we have no use for you — see how you fight your own way through.”
sentences.n: “was sollen wir mit dir?” leaves the verb out altogether: what are we to do with you. brauchen here is “to have a use for.” zusehen is to see to a thing, and “sich durchschlagen” to fight one’s way through, to get by. The blunt du is the du of family.

sentences.t: Der Soldat hatte nichts übrig als sein Gewehr, das nahm er auf die Schulter und wollte in die Welt gehen.
sentences.l: The soldier had nothing left over but his gun, that he took on the shoulder and wanted to go into the world.
sentences.i: The soldier had nothing left but his gun; he took it on his shoulder and meant to go out into the world.
sentences.n: “nichts übrig als” = nothing remaining but. Fronting das (“that”) hooks the second clause onto the gun without naming it again. “in die Welt gehen” is the tales’ phrase for going out into the wide world to look for a living.

sentences.t: Er kam auf eine große Heide, auf der nichts zu sehen war als ein Ring von Bäumen: darunter setzte er sich ganz traurig nieder und sann über sein Schicksal nach.
sentences.l: He came onto a great heath, on which nothing was to be seen but a ring of trees: under them he set himself down quite sadly and pondered over his fate.
sentences.i: He came onto a great heath where nothing was to be seen but a ring of trees; under them he sat down quite sadly and brooded over his fate.
sentences.n: “zu sehen war” is sein + zu + infinitive, with a passive sense: was to be seen. niedersetzen is separable — setzte … nieder — and “nachsinnen über” is to muse or brood over, with nach standing last. Heide is open heathland.

sentences.t: „Ich habe kein Geld,“ dachte er, „ich habe nichts gelernt als das Kriegshandwerk, und jetzt weil Friede geschlossen ist, brauchen sie mich nicht mehr; ich sehe voraus ich muß verhungern.“
sentences.l: “I have no money,” he thought, “I have learnt nothing but the war-handicraft, and now, because peace is concluded, they need me no more; I see beforehand I must starve.”
sentences.i: “I have no money,” he thought, “I have learnt nothing but soldiering, and now that peace is made they have no more need of me; I see it coming that I must starve.”
sentences.n: Kriegshandwerk is the trade of war — Handwerk is a craft learnt by apprenticeship, and the word puts soldiering among them. vorausehen, to foresee, is separable: sehe … voraus. verhungern is to die of hunger.

sentences.t: Auf einmal hörte er ein Brausen, und wie er sich umblickte, stand ein unbekannter Mann vor ihm, der einen grünen Rock trug, recht stattlich aussah, aber einen garstigen Pferdefuß hatte.
sentences.l: All at once he heard a roaring, and as he looked about him, an unknown man stood before him, who wore a green coat, looked quite stately, but had a hideous horse’s-foot.
sentences.i: All at once he heard a roaring; and when he looked round, an unknown man stood before him, wearing a green coat and looking stately enough, but with a hideous horse’s hoof.
sentences.n: “auf einmal” = all at once. Brausen is a rushing, roaring noise, of wind or water. “sich umblicken” = to look about one. The Pferdefuß gives the stranger away before the tale names him: the devil in these tales is known by his horse’s hoof, and the green coat is his too.

sentences.t: „Ich weiß schon was dir fehlt,“ sagte der Mann, „Geld und Gut sollst du haben, so viel du mit aller Gewalt durchbringen kannst, aber ich muß zuvor wissen ob du dich nicht fürchtest, damit ich mein Geld nicht umsonst ausgebe.“
sentences.l: “I know well what is lacking to you,” said the man, “money and goods you shall have, as much as you with all force can get through, but I must know beforehand whether you are not afraid, so that I do not spend my money for nothing.”
sentences.i: “I know well enough what ails you,” said the man; “money and goods you shall have, as much as you can run through with all your might; but I must first know whether you are afraid of nothing, so that I do not spend my money for nothing.”
sentences.n: “was dir fehlt” — what is wanting to you, the person in the dative. “Geld und Gut” is a fixed pair: money and property. durchbringen is to get through, and of money to run through it, squander it. “sich fürchten” = to be afraid; umsonst = for nothing, in vain.

sentences.t: „Ein Soldat und Furcht, wie paßt das zusammen?“ antwortete er, „du kannst mich auf die Probe stellen.“
sentences.l: “A soldier and fear, how does that fit together?” he answered, “you can put me to the test.”
sentences.i: “A soldier and fear — how do those go together?” he answered; “you may put me to the proof.”
sentences.n: zusammenpassen is to match, to fit together, separable: paßt … zusammen. “auf die Probe stellen” = to put to the test. He answers the stranger with du and keeps it up through the whole bargain.

sentences.t: „Wohlan,“ antwortete der Mann, „schau hinter dich.“
sentences.l: “Well then,” answered the man, “look behind you.”
sentences.n: wohlan is an old “well then, come on,” the word that opens a challenge. schau is the bare du-imperative of schauen.

sentences.t: Der Soldat kehrte sich um und sah einen großen Bär, der brummend auf ihn zutrabte.
sentences.l: The soldier turned himself round and saw a great bear that came trotting towards him growling.
sentences.i: The soldier turned round and saw a great bear trotting towards him, growling.
sentences.n: “sich umkehren” = to turn round, separable: kehrte … um. brummend is the present participle of brummen, to growl, used as English uses “growling.” “auf jemanden zutraben” = to trot towards someone.

sentences.t: „Oho,“ rief der Soldat, „dich will ich an der Nase kitzeln, daß dir die Lust zum Brummen vergehen soll,“
sentences.l: “Oho,” cried the soldier, “you I will tickle on the nose, so that the desire for growling shall pass away from you,”
sentences.i: “Oho,” cried the soldier, “I will tickle you on the nose, so that your appetite for growling shall leave you,”
sentences.n: dich is fronted in defiance, and the verb keeps its second place. “die Lust vergeht mir” = my appetite for a thing passes away, the person in the dative: dir. The tickling is grim jesting: he means the shot.

sentences.t: legte an und schoß den Bär auf die Schnauze, daß er zusammenfiel und sich nicht mehr regte.
sentences.l: [he] levelled and shot the bear on the snout, so that it fell together and stirred no more.
sentences.i: [he] took aim and shot the bear in the snout, so that it collapsed and never stirred again.
sentences.n: The subject is left out — the speech runs straight on into the deed — so the English supplies [he]; that bracket is ours, not the Grimms’. anlegen is the marksman’s word for levelling a gun, separable: legte … an. zusammenfallen is to fall in a heap; “sich regen” is to stir.

sentences.t: „Ich sehe wohl,“ sagte der Fremde, „daß dirs an Muth nicht fehlt, aber es ist noch eine Bedingung dabei, die mußt du erfüllen.“
sentences.l: “I see well,” said the stranger, “that courage is not lacking to you, but there is yet a condition with it, that you must fulfil.”
sentences.i: “I see well enough,” said the stranger, “that you are not wanting in courage; but there is one condition besides, and that you must fulfil.”
sentences.n: “es fehlt mir an etwas” = I am short of a thing, the person in the dative and the thing after an; dirs = dir es. Muth is the 1857 spelling of Mut. Fronting die (“that one”) points at the condition and holds it up.

sentences.t: „Wenn mirs an meiner Seligkeit nicht schadet,“ antwortete der Soldat, der wohl merkte wen er vor sich hatte, „sonst laß ich mich auf nichts ein.“
sentences.l: “If it does not harm me in my salvation,” answered the soldier, who well noticed whom he had before him, “otherwise I let myself in on nothing.”
sentences.i: “So long as it does no harm to my salvation,” answered the soldier, who saw well enough whom he had before him; “otherwise I will have nothing to do with it.”
sentences.n: Seligkeit is blessedness, the soul’s salvation — the one thing he will not bargain away, and the tale turns on his keeping it. schaden takes the dative of the person: mirs = mir es. “sich einlassen auf” = to let oneself in for a thing, separable: laß … ein.

sentences.t: „Das wirst du selber sehen,“ antwortete der Grünrock, „du darfst in den nächsten sieben Jahren dich nicht waschen, dir Bart und Haare nicht kämmen, die Nägel nicht schneiden und kein Vaterunser beten.
sentences.l: “That you will see yourself,” answered the green-coat, “you may not in the next seven years wash yourself, comb yourself beard and hair, cut the nails and pray no Our Father.
sentences.i: “That you shall see for yourself,” answered the green coat: “for the next seven years you may not wash yourself, nor comb your beard and hair, nor cut your nails, nor pray one Our Father.
sentences.n: Grünrock, green-coat, is the tale’s nickname for the devil, taken from the coat he wears. dürfen is to be allowed, and with nicht it forbids. “dir Bart und Haare kämmen” is the dative of possession: German says “comb to yourself the beard.” Vaterunser is the Lord’s Prayer, named from its first two words.

sentences.t: Dann will ich dir einen Rock und Mantel geben, den mußt du in dieser Zeit tragen.
sentences.l: Then I will give you a coat and cloak, that you must wear in this time.
sentences.i: Then I will give you a coat and a cloak, and that you must wear all this time.
sentences.n: den is fronted and points back to the coat, the verb keeping second place. Rock is a man’s outer coat; Mantel a cloak.

sentences.t: Stirbst du in diesen sieben Jahren, so bist du mein, bleibst du aber leben, so bist du frei und bist reich dazu für dein Lebtag.“
sentences.l: Die you in these seven years, then you are mine, but stay you alive, then you are free and are rich besides for your life-day.”
sentences.i: If you die within these seven years you are mine; but if you stay alive you are free, and rich into the bargain for the rest of your life.”
sentences.n: Two conditionals with no wenn, each with its verb first and each answered by so: die you … then; stay you alive … then. dazu = besides, into the bargain. “für dein Lebtag” = for your lifetime.

sentences.t: Der Soldat dachte an die große Noth, in der er sich befand, und da er so oft in den Tod gegangen war, wollte er es auch jetzt wagen und willigte ein.
sentences.l: The soldier thought of the great need in which he found himself, and since he had so often gone into death, he wanted to venture it now too and consented.
sentences.i: The soldier thought of the great want he was in; and since he had so often gone into death, he was willing to venture it now too, and consented.
sentences.n: “sich befinden” = to find oneself, to be in a state or place. “in den Tod gehen” is said of a soldier going where death is. wagen is to venture, to risk. einwilligen is separable: willigte … ein.

sentences.t: Der Teufel zog den grünen Rock aus, reichte ihn dem Soldaten hin und sagte, „wenn du den Rock an deinem Leibe hast und in die Tasche greifst, so wirst du die Hand immer voll Geld haben.“
sentences.l: The devil drew the green coat off, handed it over to the soldier and said, “when you have the coat on your body and reach into the pocket, then you will always have the hand full of money.”
sentences.i: The devil pulled off the green coat, handed it to the soldier and said: “when you have the coat on your body and reach into the pocket, you will always find your hand full of money.”
sentences.n: ausziehen of clothes is to take off, separable: zog … aus; hinreichen is to hand over. “an deinem Leibe” = on your body. “in die Tasche greifen” = to reach into one’s pocket. German says “die Hand,” the hand, where English says “your hand.”

sentences.t: Dann zog er dem Bären die Haut ab und sagte „das soll dein Mantel sein und auch dein Bett, denn darauf mußt du schlafen und darfst in kein anderes Bett kommen.
sentences.l: Then he drew the skin off the bear and said “that shall be your cloak and also your bed, for on it you must sleep and may come into no other bed.
sentences.i: Then he stripped the skin off the bear and said: “that shall be your cloak and your bed too, for on it you must sleep, and you may come into no other bed.
sentences.n: “jemandem die Haut abziehen” is the dative of possession once more: the bear stands in the dative, dem Bären, as owner of the skin. abziehen is separable: zog … ab. German loads the negative onto the noun — “in kein anderes Bett” — where English says “not into any other.”

sentences.t: Und dieser Tracht wegen sollst du Bärenhäuter heißen.“
sentences.l: And on account of this garb you shall be called Bearskin.”
sentences.i: And because of this garb you shall be called Bearskin.”
sentences.n: wegen follows its noun here — “dieser Tracht wegen” — the older, weightier order. Tracht is a costume, a habit of dress. Bärenhäuter is made from Bärenhaut, bear’s hide, and means a man who sleeps on one: already a byword for a slovenly idler before this tale gave it a story. The 1857 text keeps Bärenhäuter throughout; the apparatus renders the name as Bearskin so that the reader can hear what the devil is calling him.

sentences.t: Hierauf verschwand der Teufel.
sentences.l: Hereupon the devil vanished.
sentences.i: Thereupon the devil vanished.
sentences.n: hierauf = upon this, thereupon; the old compounds of hier with a preposition survive in the English “hereupon.”

sentences.t: Der Soldat zog den Rock an, griff gleich in die Tasche und fand daß die Sache ihre Richtigkeit hatte.
sentences.l: The soldier drew the coat on, reached at once into the pocket and found that the matter had its rightness.
sentences.i: The soldier put the coat on, reached at once into the pocket, and found that the thing was just as promised.
sentences.n: anziehen of clothes is to put on, separable: zog … an. “seine Richtigkeit haben” is a fixed phrase: to be in order, to be just as it should be.

sentences.t: Dann hieng er die Bärenhaut um, gieng in die Welt, war guter Dinge und unterließ nichts was ihm wohl und dem Gelde wehe that.
sentences.l: Then he hung the bear-skin about him, went into the world, was of good things and left undone nothing that did him good and the money harm.
sentences.i: Then he hung the bear skin about him, went out into the world, was of good cheer, and left undone nothing that did him good and his money harm.
sentences.n: umhängen is to hang about oneself, separable: hieng … um, and hieng is the 1857 spelling of hing. “guter Dinge sein” = to be in good spirits, of good cheer. unterlassen is to leave undone. “wohl thun” and “wehe thun” both take a dative — here the money is the sufferer, a small joke.

sentences.t: Im ersten Jahr gieng es noch leidlich, aber in dem zweiten sah er schon aus wie ein Ungeheuer.
sentences.l: In the first year it went still tolerably, but in the second he already looked like a monster.
sentences.i: In the first year it went tolerably enough, but in the second he already looked like a monster.
sentences.n: “es geht leidlich” = things go tolerably, passably. aussehen, to look, is separable: sah … aus. Ungeheuer is a monster, a thing outside nature.

sentences.t: Das Haar bedeckte ihm fast das ganze Gesicht, sein Bart glich einem Stück grobem Filztuch, seine Finger hatten Krallen, und sein Gesicht war so mit Schmutz bedeckt, daß wenn man Kresse hinein gesät hätte, sie aufgegangen wäre.
sentences.l: The hair covered him almost the whole face, his beard resembled a piece of coarse felt-cloth, his fingers had claws, and his face was so covered with dirt that if one had sown cress into it, it would have come up.
sentences.i: His hair covered almost his whole face, his beard was like a piece of coarse felt, his fingers had claws, and his face was so caked with dirt that if one had sown cress in it, the cress would have come up.
sentences.n: “bedeckte ihm das Gesicht” is the dative of possession: ihm carries the owner of the face. gleichen takes the dative: einem Stück. Filztuch is felt cloth. aufgehen of seed is to come up, to sprout; “hätte … gesät” and “wäre aufgegangen” are the subjunctive of an unreal case.

sentences.t: Wer ihn sah, lief fort, weil er aber aller Orten den Armen Geld gab, damit sie für ihn beteten daß er in den sieben Jahren nicht stürbe, und weil er alles gut bezahlte, so erhielt er doch immer noch Herberge.
sentences.l: Whoever saw him ran away, but because he gave the poor money in all places, so that they should pray for him that he might not die in the seven years, and because he paid everything well, he still got lodging after all.
sentences.i: Whoever saw him ran away; but because he gave money to the poor everywhere, that they might pray for him not to die within the seven years, and because he paid well for everything, he still found lodging all the same.
sentences.n: “aller Orten” is an old genitive phrase: in all places, everywhere. damit with its verb at the end is “so that,” and stürbe is the subjunctive after it. Herberge is shelter for the night, a lodging. doch at the end is “after all, all the same.”

sentences.t: Im vierten Jahr kam er in ein Wirthshaus, da wollte ihn der Wirth nicht aufnehmen und wollte ihm nicht einmal einen Platz im Stall anweisen, weil er fürchtete seine Pferde würden scheu werden.
sentences.l: In the fourth year he came into an inn, there the innkeeper would not take him in and would not even assign him a place in the stable, because he feared his horses would become shy.
sentences.i: In the fourth year he came to an inn, where the innkeeper would not take him in and would not even give him a place in the stable, because he feared his horses would take fright.
sentences.n: Wirthshaus (modern Wirtshaus) is an inn, and the Wirth its keeper. aufnehmen is to take someone in, anweisen to assign or allot, both separable. “scheu werden” of a horse is to shy, to take fright. würden is reported speech again.

sentences.t: Doch als der Bärenhäuter in die Tasche griff und eine Hand voll Ducaten herausholte, so ließ der Wirth sich erweichen, und gab ihm eine Stube im Hintergebäude;
sentences.l: Yet when Bearskin reached into the pocket and pulled out a handful of ducats, then the innkeeper let himself be softened, and gave him a room in the back building;
sentences.i: Yet when Bearskin reached into his pocket and pulled out a handful of ducats, the innkeeper let himself be softened, and gave him a room in the back building;
sentences.n: erweichen is to make soft, and “sich erweichen lassen” to let oneself be moved, to relent. Ducaten were gold coins. Stube is a heated room, a chamber; Hintergebäude the building at the back of the yard, away from the guests.

sentences.t: doch mußte er versprechen, sich nicht sehen zu lassen, damit sein Haus nicht in bösen Ruf käme.
sentences.l: yet he had to promise not to let himself be seen, so that his house should not come into bad repute.
sentences.i: but he had to promise not to let himself be seen, so that the house should not come into ill repute.
sentences.n: “sich sehen lassen” = to show oneself, to let oneself be seen. “in bösen Ruf kommen” = to get a bad name; Ruf is what is called about a man, his repute. käme is the subjunctive after damit.

sentences.t: Als der Bärenhäuter Abends allein saß und von Herzen wünschte daß die sieben Jahre herum wären, so hörte er in einem Nebenzimmer ein lautes Jammern.
sentences.l: When Bearskin sat alone of an evening and wished from the heart that the seven years were round, then he heard in a neighbouring room a loud lamenting.
sentences.i: When Bearskin sat alone one evening, wishing from his heart that the seven years were over, he heard a loud lamenting in the next room.
sentences.n: Abends is a genitive of time doing duty as an adverb: of an evening. “von Herzen” = from the heart, heartily. “herum sein” of time is to be up, over. Jammern is the infinitive used as a noun: a lamenting, a wailing.

sentences.t: Er hatte ein mitleidiges Herz, öffnete die Thüre und erblickte einen alten Mann, der heftig weinte und die Hände über dem Kopf zusammen schlug.
sentences.l: He had a compassionate heart, opened the door and caught sight of an old man who wept violently and struck the hands together over the head.
sentences.i: He had a compassionate heart; he opened the door and saw an old man weeping violently and wringing his hands above his head.
sentences.n: erblicken is to catch sight of, a shade more vivid than sehen. “die Hände zusammenschlagen” is the old gesture of dismay, clapping the hands together — and German again says “the hands,” “the head,” where English says “his.” Thüre is the 1857 spelling of Türe.

sentences.t: Der Bärenhäuter trat näher, aber der Mann sprang auf und wollte entfliehen.
sentences.l: Bearskin stepped nearer, but the man sprang up and wanted to flee.
sentences.i: Bearskin stepped nearer, but the man sprang up and would have fled.
sentences.n: näher is the comparative of nah. aufspringen is separable: sprang … auf. entfliehen is to flee away, to escape; wollte here is being on the point of a thing, not merely wishing it.

sentences.t: Endlich, als er eine menschliche Stimme vernahm, ließ er sich bewegen, und durch freundliches Zureden brachte es der Bärenhäuter dahin, daß er ihm die Ursache seines Kummers offenbarte.
sentences.l: At last, when he heard a human voice, he let himself be moved, and through friendly urging Bearskin brought it so far that he disclosed to him the cause of his grief.
sentences.i: At last, when he heard a human voice, he let himself be won over; and by friendly urging Bearskin brought it about that the old man told him the cause of his grief.
sentences.n: vernehmen is to perceive by hearing, a formal word. “sich bewegen lassen” = to let oneself be moved, to relent. Zureden is another infinitive used as a noun: talking to someone, urging him. “es dahin bringen, daß …” = to bring things to the point where. offenbaren is to disclose.

sentences.t: Sein Vermögen war nach und nach geschwunden, er und seine Töchter mußten darben, und er war so arm, daß er den Wirth nicht einmal bezahlen konnte und ins Gefängniß sollte gesetzt werden.
sentences.l: His property had dwindled little by little, he and his daughters had to suffer want, and he was so poor that he could not even pay the innkeeper and was to be set into prison.
sentences.i: His fortune had dwindled away little by little; he and his daughters had to go without, and he was so poor that he could not even pay the innkeeper, and was to be put in prison.
sentences.n: Vermögen is what a man is worth, his means. “nach und nach” = little by little. schwinden is to dwindle, waste away; darben is to suffer want. Gefängniß is the 1857 spelling of Gefängnis — a debt could indeed be answered with prison, so the threat is not idle.

sentences.t: „Wenn ihr weiter keine Sorgen habt,“ sagte der Bärenhäuter, „Geld habe ich genug.“
sentences.l: “If you have no further cares,” said Bearskin, “money I have enough.”
sentences.i: “If those are all your cares,” said Bearskin, “I have money enough.”
sentences.n: ihr is the respectful plural: Bearskin speaks courteously to the old man, who is a stranger to him. “weiter keine” = no other, none further. Fronting Geld puts the weight of the sentence on it: money — that I have.

sentences.t: Er ließ den Wirth herbeikommen, bezahlte ihn und steckte dem Unglücklichen noch einen Beutel voll Gold in die Tasche.
sentences.l: He had the innkeeper come up, paid him and stuck the unfortunate man besides a purse full of gold into the pocket.
sentences.i: He had the innkeeper called in, paid him, and slipped a purse full of gold into the poor man’s pocket besides.
sentences.n: “kommen lassen” is the causative: to have someone come, to send for him. der Unglückliche is an adjective used as a noun, the unfortunate one, and stands in the dative here. noch is “besides, on top of that.”

sentences.t: Als der alte Mann sich aus seinen Sorgen erlöst sah, wußte er nicht womit er sich dankbar beweisen sollte.
sentences.l: When the old man saw himself released from his cares, he did not know with what he should prove himself grateful.
sentences.i: When the old man saw himself freed from his cares, he did not know how to show his gratitude.
sentences.n: erlösen, the word these tales use for breaking a spell, serves here for release from trouble. womit = with what. “sich dankbar beweisen” = to prove oneself thankful.

sentences.t: „Komm mit mir,“ sprach er zu ihm, „meine Töchter sind Wunder von Schönheit, wähle dir eine davon zur Frau.
sentences.l: “Come with me,” he spoke to him, “my daughters are wonders of beauty, choose yourself one of them for a wife.
sentences.i: “Come with me,” he said to him; “my daughters are wonders of beauty — choose one of them for your wife.
sentences.n: mitkommen is separable, and the imperative komm mit leaves the particle at the end. “ein Wunder von Schönheit” = a wonder of beauty. “wähle dir eine” has a dative reflexive: choose one for yourself. “zur Frau” = as a wife.

sentences.t: Wenn sie hört was du für mich gethan hast, so wird sie sich nicht weigern.
sentences.l: When she hears what you have done for me, then she will not refuse.
sentences.i: When she hears what you have done for me, she will not refuse.
sentences.n: “sich weigern” = to refuse, to decline. The answering so after a wenn-clause is again dropped in English. gethan is the 1857 spelling of getan.

sentences.t: Du siehst freilich ein wenig seltsam aus, aber sie wird dich schon wieder in Ordnung bringen.“
sentences.l: You look, to be sure, a little strange, but she will bring you into order again right enough.”
sentences.i: You look a little strange, to be sure, but she will soon put you to rights again.”
sentences.n: freilich concedes the obvious: to be sure, admittedly. “in Ordnung bringen” = to put right, to set in order. schon is again the little word of confidence — she will manage it, never fear — and not “already.”

sentences.t: Dem Bärenhäuter gefiel das wohl und er gieng mit.
sentences.l: That pleased Bearskin well and he went along.
sentences.i: That pleased Bearskin well enough, and he went with him.
sentences.n: gefallen takes the dative — literally “that was pleasing to Bearskin” — and the dative stands first in the sentence. mitgehen is separable: gieng … mit.

sentences.t: Als ihn die älteste erblickte, entsetzte sie sich so gewaltig vor seinem Antlitz, daß sie aufschrie und fort lief.
sentences.l: When the eldest caught sight of him, she was so mightily horrified at his countenance that she screamed out and ran away.
sentences.i: When the eldest caught sight of him, she was so appalled at his face that she screamed out and ran away.
sentences.n: “sich entsetzen vor” = to be horrified at. Antlitz is the elevated word for the face, the countenance. aufschreien, to cry out, is separable, and stands whole at the end of its subordinate clause: aufschrie.

sentences.t: Die zweite blieb zwar stehen und betrachtete ihn, von Kopf bis zu Füßen, dann aber sprach sie „wie kann ich einen Mann nehmen, der keine menschliche Gestalt mehr hat?
sentences.l: The second did indeed stay standing and looked him over, from head down to feet, but then she spoke “how can I take a man who has no human shape any more?
sentences.i: The second did stand her ground and looked him over from head to foot; but then she said: “how can I take a husband who has no human shape left?
sentences.n: zwar grants the point before aber takes it back. “stehen bleiben” = to stop, to stay standing. betrachten is to look at attentively, to survey. “einen Mann nehmen” is the ordinary phrase for taking a husband.

sentences.t: Da gefiel mir der rasierte Bär noch besser, der einmal hier zu sehen war und sich für einen Menschen ausgab, der hatte doch einen Husarenpelz an und weiße Handschuhe.
sentences.l: Then the shaved bear pleased me better still, which was once to be seen here and gave itself out for a human being, that one had at least a hussar’s fur-jacket on and white gloves.
sentences.i: Then I liked the shaved bear better still — the one that was to be seen here once and passed itself off for a man: he at least had a hussar’s jacket on, and white gloves.
sentences.n: The shaved bear is a showman’s beast, dressed up and led about the fairs — she is measuring her suitor against a performing animal. “sich ausgeben für” = to pass oneself off as. Husarenpelz is the fur-trimmed jacket of a hussar. anhaben, to have on, is separable: hatte … an. doch here is “at any rate, at least.”

sentences.t: Wenn er nur häßlich wäre, so könnte ich mich an ihn gewöhnen.“
sentences.l: If he were only ugly, then I could get used to him.”
sentences.i: If he were merely ugly, I could get used to him.”
sentences.n: “sich gewöhnen an” = to grow accustomed to, with the accusative. wäre and könnte are the subjunctive of a case that is not so. nur here is “merely, no more than.”

sentences.t: Die jüngste aber sprach „lieber Vater, das muß ein guter Mann sein, der euch aus der Noth geholfen hat, habt ihr ihm dafür eine Braut versprochen, so muß euer Wort gehalten werden.“
sentences.l: The youngest, however, spoke “dear father, that must be a good man who has helped you out of the need, have you promised him a bride for it, then your word must be kept.”
sentences.i: But the youngest said: “dear father, he must be a good man who has helped you out of your trouble; and if you have promised him a bride for it, your word must be kept.”
sentences.n: The daughters say ihr to their father, the respectful plural of the tales. helfen takes the dative: euch. “habt ihr … versprochen” is a conditional with the verb first and no wenn, answered by so. “sein Wort halten” = to keep one’s word.

sentences.t: Es war Schade, daß das Gesicht des Bärenhäuters von Schmutz und Haaren bedeckt war, sonst hätte man sehen können wie ihm das Herz im Leibe lachte, als er diese Worte hörte.
sentences.l: It was a pity that the face of Bearskin was covered with dirt and hair, otherwise one could have seen how the heart laughed in his body when he heard these words.
sentences.i: It was a pity that Bearskin’s face was covered with dirt and hair, or one might have seen how his heart laughed within him when he heard these words.
sentences.n: “es ist schade” = it is a pity. “hätte sehen können” is the double infinitive of a past modal: could have seen. “das Herz lachte ihm im Leibe” is a set phrase for inward delight, the dative ihm carrying the owner of the heart; Leib is the body.

sentences.t: Er nahm einen Ring von seinem Finger, brach ihn entzwei und gab ihr die eine Hälfte, die andere behielt er für sich.
sentences.l: He took a ring from his finger, broke it in two and gave her the one half, the other he kept for himself.
sentences.n: entzwei = in two, apart. Fronting “die andere” sets the two halves against each other, and the verb still keeps second place.

sentences.t: In ihre Hälfte aber schrieb er seinen Namen und in seine Hälfte schrieb er ihren Namen und bat sie ihr Stück gut aufzuheben.
sentences.l: But in her half he wrote his name and in his half he wrote her name and begged her to keep her piece well.
sentences.i: But in her half he wrote his name, and in his half he wrote her name, and begged her to keep her piece safe.
sentences.n: The two halves of the sentence are built to match the two halves of the ring. aufheben is to keep, to preserve, separable, with the zu inside it: aufzuheben.

sentences.t: Hierauf nahm er Abschied und sprach „ich muß noch drei Jahre wandern.
sentences.l: Hereupon he took leave and spoke “I must wander three years more.
sentences.i: Thereupon he took his leave and said: “I must wander three years more.
sentences.n: “Abschied nehmen” = to take one’s leave — the same word that was his discharge from the army in the first paragraph. wandern is to travel on foot, to roam.

sentences.t: Komm ich aber nicht wieder, so bist du frei, weil ich dann todt bin.
sentences.l: But come I not again, then you are free, because I am then dead.
sentences.i: But if I do not come back, you are free, because then I shall be dead.
sentences.n: Another conditional with the verb first and no wenn, answered by so. wiederkommen is separable, and the particle wieder stands at the end. German keeps the present bin where English wants a future.

sentences.t: Bitte aber Gott daß er mir das Leben erhält.“
sentences.l: But pray God that he preserve me the life.”
sentences.i: But pray God that he keep me alive.”
sentences.n: bitte is the du-imperative of bitten, here “pray, entreat,” taking Gott straight as its object. “mir das Leben erhalten” has the dative of the person again, where English says “my life.”

sentences.t: Die arme Braut kleidete sich ganz schwarz, und wenn sie an ihren Bräutigam dachte, so kamen ihr die Thränen in die Augen.
sentences.l: The poor bride clothed herself all in black, and when she thought of her bridegroom, then the tears came to her into the eyes.
sentences.i: The poor bride clothed herself all in black; and when she thought of her bridegroom, the tears came into her eyes.
sentences.n: Braut and Bräutigam are the betrothed pair, so called from the promise onward and not only on the wedding day. “an jemanden denken” takes the accusative. “die Thränen kamen ihr in die Augen” is the dative of possession again; Thräne is the 1857 spelling of Träne.

sentences.t: Von ihren Schwestern ward ihr nichts als Hohn und Spott zu Theil.
sentences.l: From her sisters nothing but scorn and mockery fell to her share.
sentences.i: From her sisters she got nothing but scorn and mockery.
sentences.n: “jemandem zu Theil werden” is a fixed phrase: to fall to someone’s share, to be his portion, the person in the dative; Theil is the 1857 spelling of Teil. “Hohn und Spott” is a fixed pair. ward is the old past of werden.

sentences.t: „Nimm dich in Acht,“ sagte die älteste, „wenn du ihm die Hand reichst, so schlägt er dir mit der Tatze darauf.“
sentences.l: “Take yourself in heed,” said the eldest, “if you reach him the hand, then he strikes you with the paw on it.”
sentences.i: “Take care,” said the eldest, “if you give him your hand, he will strike it with his paw.”
sentences.n: “sich in Acht nehmen” = to be on one’s guard, to take care. Tatze is the paw of a beast. The dative dir again carries the owner of the hand struck. The sisters keep up the bear-jokes for four speeches together.

sentences.t: „Hüte dich,“ sagte die zweite, „die Bären lieben die Süßigkeit, und wenn du ihm gefällst, so frißt er dich auf.“
sentences.l: “Guard yourself,” said the second, “bears love the sweetness, and if you please him, then he eats you up.”
sentences.i: “Be on your guard,” said the second: “bears love sweet things, and if he takes a liking to you, he will eat you up.”
sentences.n: Süßigkeit is sweetness, sweet stuff. The jest turns on gefallen, to please: if you are to his taste. fressen is the verb for an animal’s eating, and auffressen to devour utterly, separable: frißt … auf.

sentences.t: „Du mußt nur immer seinen Willen thun,“ hub die älteste wieder an, „sonst fängt er an zu brummen.“
sentences.l: “You must only always do his will,” the eldest began again, “otherwise he starts to growl.”
sentences.i: “You must always do just as he wants,” the eldest began again, “or else he will start growling.”
sentences.n: “seinen Willen thun” = to do someone’s will, what he wants. anheben is an old verb for beginning to speak, with the strong past hub: hub … an. brummen is both a bear’s growl and a man’s grumbling, and she means both.

sentences.t: Und die zweite fuhr fort „aber die Hochzeit wird lustig sein, Bären die tanzen gut.“
sentences.l: And the second continued “but the wedding will be merry, bears they dance well.”
sentences.i: And the second went on: “but the wedding will be a merry one — bears dance well.”
sentences.n: fortfahren is to go on, to continue, separable: fuhr … fort. “Bären die tanzen gut” sets the noun first and then takes it up again with die, a shape of spoken German that English cannot copy. Dancing bears were a common sight at fairs, which is the point of the jest.

sentences.t: Die Braut schwieg still und ließ sich nicht irre machen.
sentences.l: The bride kept quite silent and did not let herself be made confused.
sentences.i: The bride kept silent, and would not be put off.
sentences.n: “still schweigen” doubles the silence. “sich irre machen lassen” = to let oneself be put out, made to waver; irre is astray, confused.

sentences.t: Der Bärenhäuter aber zog in der Welt herum, von einem Ort zum andern, that Gutes, wo er konnte und gab den Armen reichlich, damit sie für ihn beteten.
sentences.l: Bearskin, however, drew about in the world, from one place to the other, did good where he could and gave the poor plentifully, so that they should pray for him.
sentences.i: But Bearskin roamed about the world, from one place to another, did good where he could, and gave plentifully to the poor, that they might pray for him.
sentences.n: herumziehen is to roam about, separable: zog … herum. that is the 1857 spelling of tat. “Gutes thun” = to do good, the adjective used as a noun. beteten is the subjunctive of purpose after damit.

sentences.t: Endlich als der letzte Tag von den sieben Jahren anbrach, gieng er wieder hinaus auf die Heide, und setzte sich unter den Ring von Bäumen.
sentences.l: At last, when the last day of the seven years broke, he went out again onto the heath, and set himself under the ring of trees.
sentences.i: At last, when the last day of the seven years dawned, he went out again onto the heath and sat down under the ring of trees.
sentences.n: anbrechen of a day is to break, to dawn, separable: brach … an. hinaus marks going out away from where the speaker stands. He comes back to the very spot where the bargain was struck.

sentences.t: Nicht lange, so sauste der Wind, und der Teufel stand vor ihm und blickte ihn verdrießlich an;
sentences.l: Not long, then the wind rushed, and the devil stood before him and looked at him peevishly;
sentences.i: It was not long before the wind rushed, and the devil stood before him and looked at him sourly;
sentences.n: “nicht lange, so …” has no verb at all — not long, and then; English must supply “it was not long before.” sausen is to rush, to whistle, of wind. anblicken is separable: blickte … an. verdrießlich is sullen, put out.

sentences.t: dann warf er ihm den alten Rock hin und verlangte seinen grünen zurück.
sentences.l: then he threw him the old coat down and demanded his green one back.
sentences.i: then he threw the old coat down to him and demanded his green one back.
sentences.n: hinwerfen is to throw down, separable: warf … hin, with the dative ihm for the man it is thrown to. zurückverlangen is to demand back, zurück standing last. “seinen grünen” leaves the noun out: his green one.

sentences.t: „So weit sind wir noch nicht,“ antwortete der Bärenhäuter, „erst sollst du mich reinigen.“
sentences.l: “So far we are not yet,” answered Bearskin, “first you shall clean me.”
sentences.i: “We are not so far as that yet,” answered Bearskin; “first you shall make me clean.”
sentences.n: “so weit sind wir noch nicht” = we have not got that far yet. erst = first, before anything else. reinigen is to make clean, from rein; and with the word the soldier turns the devil into his servant.

sentences.t: Der Teufel mochte wollen oder nicht, er mußte Wasser holen, den Bärenhäuter abwaschen, ihm die Haare kämmen, und die Nägel schneiden.
sentences.l: The devil might want to or not, he had to fetch water, wash Bearskin off, comb him the hair, and cut the nails.
sentences.i: Whether the devil liked it or not, he had to fetch water, wash Bearskin, comb his hair and cut his nails.
sentences.n: “er mochte wollen oder nicht” is a fixed concessive shape: like it or not. abwaschen is to wash off. “ihm die Haare kämmen” is the dative of possession once more, and “die Nägel” runs on the same construction: German says “the hair,” “the nails,” and lets the dative say whose.

sentences.t: Hierauf sah er wie ein tapferer Kriegsmann aus, und war viel schöner als je vorher.
sentences.l: Hereupon he looked like a brave war-man, and was much handsomer than ever before.
sentences.i: Thereupon he looked like a brave soldier, and was far handsomer than ever before.
sentences.n: Kriegsmann is Krieg (war) plus Mann — the old word for a soldier, a fighting man; the hyphenated “war-man” keeps the compound visible, since the English “man-of-war” means a ship. aussehen is separable, and the whole comparison is caught between sah and aus.

sentences.t: Als der Teufel glücklich abgezogen war, so war es dem Bärenhäuter ganz leicht ums Herz.
sentences.l: When the devil had happily drawn off, then it was quite light around the heart for Bearskin.
sentences.i: When the devil had safely taken himself off, Bearskin’s heart was quite light.
sentences.n: glücklich here is “safely, and none too soon,” rather than “happily.” abziehen of a person is to march off, to decamp. “es ist mir leicht ums Herz” = my heart is light, the person in the dative: dem Bärenhäuter.

sentences.t: Er gieng in die Stadt, that einen prächtigen Sammetrock an, setzte sich in einen Wagen mit vier Schimmeln bespannt und fuhr zu dem Haus seiner Braut.
sentences.l: He went into the town, put a splendid velvet coat on, set himself in a carriage harnessed with four white horses and drove to the house of his bride.
sentences.i: He went into the town, put on a splendid velvet coat, seated himself in a carriage drawn by four white horses, and drove to the house of his bride.
sentences.n: “einen Rock anthun” is the older way of saying anziehen, to put a garment on: that … an. Sammetrock is a coat of velvet (Sammet, modern Samt). Schimmel is a white or grey horse; bespannt is harnessed to.

sentences.t: Niemand erkannte ihn, der Vater hielt ihn für einen vornehmen Feldobrist und führte ihn in das Zimmer, wo seine Töchter saßen.
sentences.l: Nobody recognised him, the father took him for a distinguished field-colonel and led him into the room where his daughters sat.
sentences.i: No one recognised him; the father took him for a colonel of high rank and led him into the room where his daughters sat.
sentences.n: “halten für” = to take someone for, to consider him. vornehm is of high rank, distinguished. Feldobrist is the older form of Feldoberst, a field colonel — a great man, which is why the father makes so much of him.

sentences.t: Er mußte sich zwischen den beiden ältesten niederlassen: sie schenkten ihm Wein ein, legten ihm die besten Bissen vor und meinten sie hätten keinen schönern Mann auf der Welt gesehen.
sentences.l: He had to seat himself between the two eldest: they poured him wine in, laid the best morsels before him and thought they had seen no handsomer man in the world.
sentences.i: He had to take his seat between the two eldest; they poured out wine for him, laid the best morsels before him, and thought they had never seen a handsomer man in all the world.
sentences.n: “sich niederlassen” = to seat oneself, to settle, separable. einschenken is to pour out a drink, vorlegen to serve someone at table — both separable, both with the dative ihm. schönern is the older spelling of schöneren.

sentences.t: Die Braut aber saß in schwarzem Kleide ihm gegenüber, schlug die Augen nicht auf und sprach kein Wort.
sentences.l: The bride, however, sat in a black dress opposite him, did not raise the eyes and spoke no word.
sentences.i: But the bride sat opposite him in her black dress, never raised her eyes and spoke no word.
sentences.n: gegenüber follows its noun: ihm gegenüber, opposite him. “die Augen aufschlagen” = to raise one’s eyes, to look up; separable, and again “die Augen” where English says “her eyes.”

sentences.t: Als er endlich den Vater fragte, ob er ihm eine seiner Töchter zur Frau geben wollte, so sprangen die beiden ältesten auf, liefen in ihre Kammer und wollten prächtige Kleider anziehen, denn eine jede bildete sich ein sie wäre die Auserwählte.
sentences.l: When he at last asked the father whether he would give him one of his daughters for a wife, then the two eldest sprang up, ran into their chamber and wanted to put splendid clothes on, for each one imagined to herself she was the chosen one.
sentences.i: When at last he asked the father whether he would give him one of his daughters to wife, the two eldest sprang up and ran into their chamber to put on splendid clothes, for each one fancied that she was the chosen one.
sentences.n: “sich einbilden” = to imagine, to fancy, with a dative reflexive and separable: bildete … ein. “eine jede” = each one. die Auserwählte is the chosen one, from auserwählen, to pick out. wäre is her thought reported, not the fact.

sentences.t: Der Fremde, sobald er mit seiner Braut allein war, holte den halben Ring hervor und warf ihn in einen Becher mit Wein, den er ihr über den Tisch reichte.
sentences.l: The stranger, as soon as he was alone with his bride, fetched the half ring out and threw it into a cup with wine, which he handed her over the table.
sentences.i: The stranger, as soon as he was alone with his bride, brought out the half ring and threw it into a cup of wine, which he handed her across the table.
sentences.n: hervorholen is to bring out, separable: holte … hervor. German says “der halbe Ring,” the half ring, where English says the half of the ring. reichen is to hand, to pass.

sentences.t: Sie nahm ihn an, aber als sie getrunken hatte und den halben Ring auf dem Grund liegen fand, so schlug ihr das Herz.
sentences.l: She took it, but when she had drunk and found the half ring lying on the bottom, then her heart beat.
sentences.i: She accepted it; but when she had drunk, and found the half ring lying at the bottom, her heart beat fast.
sentences.n: annehmen is to accept, to take what is offered, separable: nahm … an. Grund is the bottom of a vessel. finden takes a bare infinitive as English does: found it lying. “ihr schlug das Herz” — the dative again for the owner of the heart.

sentences.t: Sie holte die andere Hälfte, die sie an einem Band um den Hals trug, hielt sie daran, und es zeigte sich daß beide Theile vollkommen zu einander paßten.
sentences.l: She fetched the other half, which she wore on a ribbon round the neck, held it against it, and it showed itself that both parts fitted perfectly to one another.
sentences.i: She fetched the other half, which she wore on a ribbon round her neck, held it against the first, and it proved that the two parts fitted perfectly together.
sentences.n: Band is a ribbon, a band. “daran halten” = to hold against it. “es zeigte sich” = it turned out, it was seen. “zu einander passen” = to fit together, to match; Theile is the 1857 spelling of Teile.

sentences.t: Da sprach er „ich bin dein verlobter Bräutigam, den du als Bärenhäuter gesehen hast, aber durch Gottes Gnade habe ich meine menschliche Gestalt wieder erhalten, und bin wieder rein geworden.“
sentences.l: Then he spoke “I am your betrothed bridegroom, whom you have seen as Bearskin, but through God’s grace I have received my human shape again, and have become clean again.”
sentences.i: Then he said: “I am your betrothed bridegroom, whom you saw as Bearskin; but by God’s grace I have my human shape again, and am clean once more.”
sentences.n: verlobt is betrothed, promised in marriage. “durch Gottes Gnade” = by God’s grace: the one condition he refused to sell at the beginning is what stands him in stead at the end. erhalten here is to receive, to get.

sentences.t: Er gieng auf sie zu, umarmte sie und gab ihr einen Kuß.
sentences.l: He went up to her, embraced her and gave her a kiss.
sentences.n: “auf jemanden zugehen” = to go up to someone, separable, with zu standing last. umarmen is to take in one’s arms, from Arm.

sentences.t: Indem kamen die beiden Schwestern in vollem Putz herein, und als sie sahen daß der schöne Mann der jüngsten zu Theil geworden war, und hörten daß das der Bärenhäuter war, liefen sie voll Zorn und Wuth hinaus;
sentences.l: Meanwhile the two sisters came in in full finery, and when they saw that the handsome man had fallen to the youngest’s share, and heard that that was Bearskin, they ran out full of anger and rage;
sentences.i: Just then the two sisters came in in full finery; and when they saw that the handsome man had fallen to the youngest, and heard that this was Bearskin, they ran out full of anger and fury;
sentences.n: indem here is the old adverb “meanwhile, just then,” not the modern conjunction. Putz is finery, fine dress. “jemandem zu Theil werden” is the same phrase that brought the youngest nothing but scorn a page earlier; now the portion falls the other way.

sentences.t: die eine ersäufte sich im Brunnen, die andere erhenkte sich an einem Baum.
sentences.l: the one drowned herself in the well, the other hanged herself on a tree.
sentences.i: the one drowned herself in the well, the other hanged herself from a tree.
sentences.n: ersäufen is to drown; erhenken is the older form of erhängen, to hang. The tale reports both deaths in one flat line and softens neither.

sentences.t: Am Abend klopfte jemand an der Thüre, und als der Bräutigam öffnete, so wars der Teufel im grünen Rock, der sprach „siehst du, nun habe ich zwei Seelen für deine eine.“
sentences.l: In the evening someone knocked at the door, and when the bridegroom opened, then it was the devil in the green coat, who spoke “you see, now I have two souls for your one.”
sentences.i: In the evening someone knocked at the door; and when the bridegroom opened it, there stood the devil in the green coat, who said: “you see, now I have two souls for your one.”
sentences.n: wars = war es. “an der Thüre klopfen” = to knock at the door. The devil’s last line settles the bargain his own way — he loses the soldier and takes the two sisters instead — and the tale ends on it without comment.

glossary.arm: arm — poor, destitute (adjective; not der Arm, the arm)
glossary.band: das Band — a ribbon, a band (here worn round the neck)
glossary.fuhr: fahren — went, drove (3rd sg. past; ‘fuhr fort’ = fortfahren, went on, continued)
glossary.gesetzt: setzen — set, put (past participle; ‘ins Gefängniß gesetzt werden’ = to be put in prison)
glossary.heißen: heißen — to be called, to bear a name (verb; not heiß, hot)
glossary.hohn: der Hohn — scorn, derision (‘Hohn und Spott’, a fixed pair)
glossary.kehrte: umkehren — turned round (3rd sg. past; separable: kehrte … um, with sich)
glossary.schau: schauen — look (du-imperative; ‘schau hinter dich’ = look behind you)
glossary.soldaten: der Soldat — soldier (dat. sg.; weak masculine, Soldat/Soldaten)
glossary.stube: die Stube — a heated room, a chamber
glossary.ungeheuer: das Ungeheuer — a monster, a thing outside nature (noun)
